name: Neck curls with plate

lead: Neck curls with a plate are a weighted forward bend of the neck meant to build the muscles at the front and sides of the neck. Forum users do them for a thicker neck and a more masculine overall look, and post progress photos; some also claim jaw and facial changes.

Resistance on neck flexion works the sternocleidomastoid, which bends the neck forward when both sides contract. Material on the exercise comes from forum discussion, and no clinical trial of loaded neck curls for appearance is available.

paras: Users lift or hold a weight plate on the head while bending the neck forward, as part of a lifting routine, with results reported over weeks to months of regular training.
Forum members report multi-day soreness, and one reported dizziness and nausea. No clinical safety data on loaded neck curls for appearance are available.

chain: Front and side neck muscles grow
angle.text: Forum users perform loaded neck curls with a plate to grow the front and side neck muscles for a thicker neck and a more masculine frame, with some also claiming jaw and facial changes. The exercise is popular on forums, with no trials on appearance.

lead: Neck curls with a plate are a form of loaded neck flexion: a person lifts or holds a weight plate on the head while bending the neck forward, aiming to thicken the muscles at the front and sides of the neck. In looksmaxxing forums the exercise is discussed as a way to build a thicker, more muscular neck and, by extension, a more masculine overall look from the shoulders up, and members post progress photos under labels such as "facial exercises".

The sternocleidomastoid, the large muscle running from the breastbone and collarbone to the skull behind the ear, bends the neck forward when both sides contract, and it is one of the largest superficial neck muscles.[1] Wikipedia's neck article reports average neck circumference of about 38.7 cm in men and 33.3 cm in women, which it attributes mainly to differences in body composition, muscle mass and testosterone.[2] Looksmaxxing communities treat neck thickness as part of that dimorphism and train it accordingly, often alongside jaw and posture work.

Published research on loaded neck curls as an appearance exercise is not available. The related literature concerns neck strength in sports-injury prevention, neck-pain rehabilitation and posture, and training logs on strength forums show neck work as routine accessory training.[3][4][5][6]

Thicker neck; sometimes jaw and facial claims

paras: The sternocleidomastoid runs from the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process behind the ear, and bends the neck forward when both sides contract together.[1] Loaded neck curls place resistance on this movement, typically by holding a plate against the forehead or head.

Acting alone, one sternocleidomastoid turns the head to the opposite side and tilts it toward its own side, while both together flex the neck forward and help with forced inhalation.[1] It is supplied mainly by the accessory nerve, and because it is thick it divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles.[1] Wikipedia's neck article places the sternocleidomastoid, trapezius and scalenes in the posterior triangle, with the trapezius forming the sloping outline between neck and shoulder.[2] Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article lists a defined jawline among features that communities judge when rating attractiveness, which is one reason neck and jaw work are often discussed together.[7]

Neck circumference is a visible marker of upper-body muscle. Wikipedia attributes the roughly 5 cm average difference between men and women to body composition, muscle mass and testosterone, which promotes muscle growth including in the neck.[2] The same article notes that the Adam's apple is usually more prominent in men and that neck lines develop in adulthood from sun damage, weight or ageing.[2] The posterior and lateral muscles also shape the line from ear to shoulder, which is why trapezius and neck-extension work often appear in the same routines as curls.[2][3]

Wikipedia's article on forward head posture describes a head carried forward of the shoulders with a poked-forward chin, and lists strengthening of the deep neck flexors, shoulder-blade retractors and middle and lower back among suggested approaches, while noting several of these recommendations are tagged as needing independent confirmation.[8] Members who combine neck curls with chin tucks often frame both as posture and jaw-definition work.

Training logs on T Nation, a strength-training forum, show neck work in several forms: one log lists a neck harness and neck curls in a daily circuit, another programmes "neck curls/extensions" for 3 sets of 20 repetitions in a hypertrophy circuit, and a poster suggests lifters do some neck curl or bridge work so the neck does not look weak.[3][4][5] These examples show neck training as routine accessory work in strength communities as well as in looksmaxxing ones.

Bridging, in which a person supports body weight through the feet and head or neck, appears in wrestling, judo, jiu-jitsu and other combat sports and is also used in gymnastics, according to Wikipedia's article on the bridge exercise, which describes it mainly as a lower-back and glute exercise.[9] Wikipedia notes that a larger neck circumference is associated with cardiometabolic risk and that upper-body fat is considered a worse predictor than lower-body fat; it does not discuss neck training.[2]

Neck strength has been studied mainly in sport. A 2021 scoping review of 11 studies on physical conditioning to reduce concussion risk, mostly in adolescents, examined neck strength, neck size and cervical stiffness as modifiable risk factors and found limited and conflicting evidence from small samples.[6] A 2024 study of 380 adult amateur soccer players found that neck strength and head and neck dimensions did not moderate the link between heading exposure and cognitive performance.[10] These studies concern injury prevention rather than appearance.

Conditions of the sternocleidomastoid include torticollis, in which overactive contraction tilts the head and physiotherapy stretches the affected side and strengthens the opposite side.[1] Wikipedia lists whiplash, cervical disc herniation, spinal stenosis and vascular causes among common sources of neck pain.[2] In looksmaxxing forums, members report multi-day soreness after resuming neck curls, and one poster described dizziness, nausea and chills after two sets, with replies suggesting reflux as a possible cause. No clinical data on loaded neck curls for appearance are available; forum reports are individual accounts.

Members post before-and-after photos attributed to neck curls and ask how long the person trained. Beginners describe sets of around twenty repetitions as exhausting, and one member reports several days of soreness when turning the head after resuming the exercise. Others ask whether curls enlarge the trapezius as well as the sternocleidomastoid.

Several threads ask whether neck curls and chin tucks help the jaw or face, with participants disagreeing about whether they are useful. Looksmaxxing as a whole, as described by Wikipedia, spans skincare and gym training through to cosmetic surgery, and exercise-based methods such as neck work sit at the low-cost end of that range.[7]

No studies found. Related research on neck strength in sports-injury prevention and on cervical exercise for pain exists, but no trial has tested weighted neck curls for neck size or facial appearance.[6][10]
